title: One Cable Too Many
story: A small office network has n devices, numbered 0 to n - 1. It used to be wired as a tree: every device reachable from every other, with no loops. Then someone plugged in one extra cable, and now packets circle round a loop and the switches complain.

The installer's log lists every cable in the order it was plugged in. You need to pick one cable to unplug so the network is a tree again. Several cables on the loop would work; the installer asks for the one that went in latest.
task: Write cableToUnplug(n, cables). cables has exactly n entries, each [a, b] joining devices a and b. It is a tree on all n devices plus one extra cable.
Return the cable whose removal leaves a tree. If several cables qualify, return the one that appears last in cables. Return it exactly as written in the list.
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n, a ≠ b, and no two cables join the same pair of devices
Removing some cable leaves every device connected with no loop

examples.explanation: The loop is 0-1-2-0. Unplugging any of its three cables leaves a tree. Of those, [2, 0] is the latest in the log. [2, 3] comes later, but it is not on the loop: unplugging it would cut device 3 off.
The loop is 1-2-3-4-1, made of [1, 2], [3, 4], [2, 3] and [4, 1]. The latest of those is [4, 1].

hints: Plug the cables of the first example in one at a time, in log order. At which moment does a loop first appear?
A cable creates a loop exactly when its two devices are already connected by the cables plugged in before it. And the loop appears at the moment its last cable goes in, so that cable is the answer.
So you need to keep track of which devices are already connected as cables arrive, and answer "are these two connected?" quickly. Which structure is built for exactly that?
Use union-find. Go through the cables in order. For each [a, b], find both leaders. If they are the same, a and b were already connected: return this cable. Otherwise merge the two groups.
bruteForce: Try removing each cable, starting from the end of the log, and check whether the rest is still connected, for example with a depth-first search. Return the first one that works.

Each check walks the whole network, so this costs O(n²). With 1,000 devices that is around a million steps: fine here, but it does the same connectivity work over and over. Union-find gets the answer in one pass.

walkthrough: The network has exactly one loop, and only cables on that loop can be removed. Replay the log: before the loop is complete, every cable joins two devices that were not yet connected. The cable that completes the loop is the first one whose two ends are already connected, and since it completes the loop it is also the latest loop cable in the log. So the first cable that joins two already-connected devices is the answer.
A common slip is to return the last cable in the whole log. That only works when the loop happens to close at the end. In the first example the last cable, [2, 3], is a bridge to device 3.
solution.timeWhy: n cables, each doing two finds. Path shortening keeps each find at O(log n) amortized, and in practice it is close to constant.
solution.takeaway: To find the edge that first closes a loop, add edges one by one with union-find. The first edge whose ends already share a leader is the one that creates the cycle.
